About the author: Laurence van Cott Niven is an American science fiction writer. His 1970 novel Ringworld won the Hugo, Locus, Ditmar, and Nebula awards. With Jerry Pournelle he wrote The Mote in God's Eye (1974) and Lucifer's Hammer (1977). The Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America gave him the 2015 Damon Knight Memorial Grand Master Award.

title: Getting It Done: How to Lead When You're Not In Charge
author: John Richardson and Roger Fisher
text: Published 1999. Genre: Business & Economics. This book offers strategies for leading effectively in environments where formal authority is lacking. It focuses on collaboration, negotiation, and influence, providing practical advice for achieving results through teamwork and shared goals. The authors draw on their expertise in negotiation and management to guide readers in navigating complex organizational dynamics. Tone and style: practical, straightforward, instructional. Pacing: focused, solution-oriented. Themes: leadership, collaboration, influence. Setting: contemporary organizational environments. About the author: Roger D. Fisher was a Samuel Williston Professor of Law at Harvard Law School and director of the Harvard Negotiation Project.

title: Give and Take
author: Adam Grant
text: Published 2013. Genre: Business & Economics. In 'Give and Take', Adam Grant explores how the way we interact with others influences our success. He categorizes people as givers, takers, or matchers and discusses how these styles impact personal and professional outcomes. The book presents research findings that highlight the importance of collaboration and generosity in achieving long-term success. Tone and style: insightful, engaging, research-driven. Pacing: structured, evidence-based. Themes: success, collaboration, interpersonal dynamics. Setting: contemporary organizational psychology. About the author: Adam M. Grant is an American popular science author, and professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania specializing in organizational psychology.

title: Washington Black
author: Esi Edugyan
text: Published 2018. Genre: Historical Fiction. Washington Black follows the journey of an eleven-year-old slave named George Washington Black, or Wash, on a Barbados sugar plantation. Chosen as a servant by his master's abolitionist brother, Christopher Wilde, Wash is introduced to a world of exploration and invention, including a flying machine. After a tragic event forces them to flee, Wash embarks on a global journey of self-discovery, grappling with themes of identity, freedom, and the complexities of human relationships. Tone and style: lyrical, evocative, introspective. Pacing: adventurous, character-driven. Themes: slavery, freedom, identity, exploration, betrayal. Setting: 19th-century Caribbean and beyond. About the author: Esi Edugyan is a Canadian novelist. She has twice won the Giller Prize, for her novels Half-Blood Blues (2011) and Washington Black (2018).

title: Stories of Your Life and Others
author: Ted Chiang
text: Published 2002. Genre: Science Fiction. This collection features Ted Chiang's thought-provoking short stories that explore complex themes through speculative scenarios. Notable stories include 'Tower of Babylon,' which imagines a monumental construction project reaching the heavens, and 'Story of Your Life,' which delves into the relationship between language and perception of time. Chiang's work often challenges fundamental concepts in mathematics, belief, and reality. Tone and style: intellectually engaging, lyrical prose. Pacing: varied, contemplative. Themes: language, perception, reality, belief, mathematics. Setting: various speculative scenarios and alternate realities. About the author: Ted Chiang is an American science fiction writer, whose work has won four Nebula awards, four Hugo awards, the John W. Campbell Award for Best New Writer, and six Locus awards. He has published the short story collections Stories of Your Life and Others (2002) and Exhalation: Stories (2019). His short story "Story of Your Life" was the basis of the film Arrival (2016). He was an artist in residence at the University of Notre Dame from 2020 to 2021. Chiang is also a frequent non-fiction contributor to the New Yorker, where he writes on topics related to computing such as artificial intelligence.

title: The Killing Moon
author: N.K. Jemisin
text: Published 2012. Genre: Fantasy. In the ancient city-state of Gujaareh, peace is maintained by the Gatherers, priest-assassins who harvest the magic of dreams to heal or eliminate those deemed corrupt. When a conspiracy threatens the city's stability, Ehiru, the most renowned Gatherer, must confront his beliefs and protect a woman he was meant to kill, as a dark force begins to murder dreamers in the name of the goddess of dreams. Tone and style: lyrical, immersive, thought-provoking. Pacing: steady, character-driven. Themes: power, morality, dreams, corruption. Setting: ancient city-state of Gujaareh. About the author: Nora Keita Jemisin is an American science fiction and fantasy writer. Her fiction includes a wide range of themes, notably cultural conflict and oppression. Her debut novel, The Hundred Thousand Kingdoms (2010), and the subsequent books in her Inheritance Trilogy received critical acclaim.

title: The Underground Railroad
author: Colson Whitehead
text: Published 2000. Genre: Historical Fiction. The Underground Railroad follows Cora, a young enslaved woman on a Georgia cotton plantation, who escapes with another slave named Caesar. In this alternate history, the Underground Railroad is depicted as a real railway system, leading Cora through various states where she faces both challenges and revelations about freedom and her identity. The novel explores themes of slavery, race, and the enduring impact of America's past. Tone and style: lyrical, poignant, immersive. Pacing: fast-paced, episodic. Themes: freedom, slavery, identity, race. Setting: antebellum South, various states in America. About the author: Arch Colson Chipp Whitehead is an American novelist. He is the author of ten novels, including his 1999 debut The Intuitionist; The Underground Railroad (2016), for which he won the 2016 National Book Award for Fiction and the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; and The Nickel Boys, for which he won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction again in 2020, making him one of only four writers ever to win the prize twice. He has also published two books of nonfiction. In 2002, he received a MacArthur Fellowship.

title: Exhalation
author: Ted Chiang
text: Published 2014. Genre: Science Fiction. Exhalation is a collection of nine short stories that explore deep philosophical questions and speculative ideas. The narratives range from a time-traveling merchant in ancient Baghdad to an alien scientist's discovery about the universe, each story tackling themes of choice, free will, and the nature of existence. The collection showcases Ted Chiang's ability to weave profound concepts into engaging narratives. Tone and style: thought-provoking, lyrical, speculative. Pacing: varied, reflective. Themes: choice, free will, existence, time travel, alternate realities. Setting: various speculative contexts, including ancient Baghdad and alien worlds. About the author: Ted Chiang is an American science fiction writer, whose work has won four Nebula awards, four Hugo awards, the John W. Campbell Award for Best New Writer, and six Locus awards. He has published the short story collections Stories of Your Life and Others (2002) and Exhalation: Stories (2019). His short story "Story of Your Life" was the basis of the film Arrival (2016). He was an artist in residence at the University of Notre Dame from 2020 to 2021. Chiang is also a frequent non-fiction contributor to the New Yorker, where he writes on topics related to computing such as artificial intelligence.

title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Harari
text: Published 2011. Genre: History. Sapiens explores the history of humankind from the emergence of Homo sapiens to modern society. Harari examines how our species evolved, created complex societies, and developed shared beliefs in constructs like money and nations. The book integrates insights from various disciplines to challenge conventional understandings of human behavior and societal development. Tone and style: bold, provocative, interdisciplinary. Pacing: wide-ranging, analytical. Themes: evolution, society, belief systems, human behavior. Setting: the history of humankind from prehistory to the present. About the author: Yuval Noah Harari is an Israeli medievalist, military historian, public intellectual, and popular science writer. He is a professor of history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. His first bestselling book, Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (2011) is based on his lectures to an undergraduate world history class. His other works include the bestsellers Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow (2016), 21 Lessons for the 21st Century (2018), and Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI (2024). His published work examines themes of free will, consciousness, intelligence, happiness, suffering and the role of storytelling in human evolution.

title: Expecting Better
author: Emily Oster
text: Published 2013. Genre: Health & Wellness. Emily Oster's "Expecting Better" challenges conventional pregnancy guidelines by critically analyzing the data behind common recommendations. The book empowers expectant mothers to make informed choices about their health and lifestyle during pregnancy, addressing topics such as caffeine consumption and prenatal testing. Oster aims to demystify the experience of pregnancy, providing evidence-based insights to help women navigate this significant life event. Tone and style: informal, accessible, evidence-based. Pacing: structured, data-driven. Themes: pregnancy, informed choice, health myths. Setting: contemporary pregnancy and maternal health context. About the author: Emily Fair Oster is an American economist who has served since 2019 as the Royce Family Professor of Teaching Excellence at Brown University, where she has been a professor of economics since 2015. Her research interests span from development economics and health economics to research design and experimental methodology. Her research was brought to the attention of non-economists through The Wall Street Journal, the book SuperFreakonomics, and her 2007 TED Talk.

title: Childhood's End
author: Arthur C. Clarke
text: Published 1952. Genre: Science Fiction. In 'Childhood's End', alien Overlords arrive on Earth, bringing an era of peace and prosperity while secretly guiding humanity toward a predetermined evolution. As the Overlords eliminate conflict and suffering, human culture stagnates, revealing the darker implications of their seemingly benevolent rule. Ultimately, the true purpose of the Overlords becomes apparent, raising questions about the future of humanity. Tone and style: thought-provoking, speculative, analytical. Pacing: measured, philosophical. Themes: human evolution, utopia vs dystopia, the nature of progress. Setting: near-future Earth under alien supervision. About the author: Sir Arthur Charles Clarke was an English science fiction writer, science writer, futurist, inventor, undersea explorer, and television series host.

title: Home Remedies
author: Xuan Juliana Wang
text: Published 2019. Genre: Short Stories. Home Remedies is a collection of short stories that explores the experiences of Chinese youth, particularly second-generation immigrants. The stories delve into themes of love, family, and identity, presenting a diverse range of characters and their struggles with belonging in a modern context. Through inventive storytelling, Xuan Juliana Wang captures the complexities of the immigrant experience and the aspirations of a new generation. Tone and style: empathetic, imaginative, contemporary. Pacing: varied, character-driven. Themes: identity, belonging, immigrant experience. Setting: contemporary Chinese-American culture. About the author: Xuan Juliana Wang is a Chinese American writer. She teaches creative writing at the University of California, Los Angeles. Her 2019 short story collection, Home Remedies, won the John C. Zacharis First Book Award and was shortlisted for the Young Lions Fiction Award and the 2020 PEN/Robert W. Bingham Prize. She earned her MFA from Columbia University and received a Stegner Fellowship to study at Stanford University.

title: The Wild Shore
author: Kim Stanley Robinson
text: Published 1984. Genre: Science Fiction. The Wild Shore follows a young man's journey of self-discovery on the Pacific coast after a nuclear war has reshaped society. Set in a post-apocalyptic California, the narrative explores themes of survival, community, and the impact of environmental disaster. It is the first book in the 'Three Californias' trilogy, which examines different possible futures for the region. Tone and style: lyrical, reflective, character-focused. Pacing: slow-burn, introspective. Themes: survival, community, environmental disaster. Setting: post-apocalyptic California. About the author: Kim Stanley Robinson is an American science fiction writer best known for his Mars trilogy of novels. Many of his novels and stories have ecological, cultural, and political themes, featuring scientists as heroes. Robinson has won numerous awards, including the Hugo Award for Best Novel, the Nebula Award for Best Novel, and the World Fantasy Award. The Atlantic magazine has called Robinson's work "the gold standard of realistic, and highly literary, science-fiction writing." According to The New Yorker magazine, Robinson is "generally acknowledged as one of the greatest living science-fiction writers."

title: Cribsheet
author: Emily Oster
text: Published 2019. Genre: Self-Help & Personal Development. Cribsheet explores the complexities of parenting advice, emphasizing that there is no universal solution for every family. Through evidence-based insights from child development and behavioral economics, the author argues against the myth of the 'perfect parent' and advocates for 'good enough' parenting. The book provides practical strategies for navigating common parenting challenges, highlighting the importance of flexibility and informed decision-making. Tone and style: informative, supportive, conversational. Pacing: structured, evidence-based. Themes: parenting, child development, societal pressure. Setting: contemporary parenting landscape. About the author: Emily Fair Oster is an American economist who has served since 2019 as the Royce Family Professor of Teaching Excellence at Brown University, where she has been a professor of economics since 2015. Her research interests span from development economics and health economics to research design and experimental methodology. Her research was brought to the attention of non-economists through The Wall Street Journal, the book SuperFreakonomics, and her 2007 TED Talk.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
text: Published 1813. Genre: Literary Fiction. Pride and Prejudice follows Elizabeth Bennet as she navigates issues of class, marriage, and morality in early 19th-century England. The novel centers on her interactions with the wealthy Mr. Darcy and explores themes of social status and personal growth. Through Elizabeth's journey, Austen critiques the societal norms of her time. Tone and style: witty, elegant, satirical. Pacing: moderate, character-driven. Themes: class, marriage, individuality, social expectations. Setting: early 19th-century England. About the author: Jane Austen was an English writer known primarily for her six novels, which implicitly interpret, critique, and comment on the English landed gentry at the end of the 18th century.

title: The Reactionary Mind
author: Corey Robin
text: Published 2011. Genre: Politics & Current Affairs. In The Reactionary Mind, Corey Robin explores the roots and motivations of conservatism, tracing its development from the reaction against the French Revolution to contemporary political figures. He argues that conservatives are united by their defense of power and privilege against movements for freedom and equality, while also adapting to new challenges. The book examines the dynamic nature of conservative ideologies and their historical context, providing insights into their appeal and resilience. Tone and style: analytical, critical, engaging. Pacing: methodical, argument-driven. Themes: conservatism, power dynamics, political ideology. Setting: historical and contemporary political landscape. About the author: Corey Robin is an American political theorist, journalist and professor of political science at Brooklyn College and the Graduate Center of the City University of New York. He has written books on the role of fear in political life, tracing its presence from Aristotle through the war on terror, and on the nature of conservatism in the modern world, from Edmund Burke to Donald Trump. Most recently, he is the author of a study of Justice Clarence Thomas that argues that the mainspring of Thomas's jurisprudence is a combination of black nationalism and black conservatism.

title: Virtual Light
author: William Gibson
text: Published 1743. Genre: Science Fiction. Set in a post-apocalyptic California, 'Virtual Light' follows Berry Rydell, a former security officer turned bounty hunter, and Chevette Washington, a bicycle messenger who steals a pair of high-tech sunglasses. These sunglasses reveal valuable information that puts them in danger as they navigate a world where data is the ultimate currency. Their journey leads them to the heart of DatAmerica, exploring the intersections of technology and society. Tone and style: stylish, gritty, fast-paced. Pacing: fast-paced, plot-driven. Themes: technology, survival, information age. Setting: post-apocalyptic California. About the author: William Ford Gibson is an American and Canadian speculative fiction writer and essayist widely credited with pioneering the science fiction subgenre known as cyberpunk, a category from which he has repeatedly distanced himself. Beginning his writing career in the late 1970s, his early works were noir, near-future stories that explored the effects of technology, cybernetics, and computer networks on humans, a "combination of lowlife and high tech"—and helped to create an iconography for the Information Age before the ubiquity of the Internet in the 1990s. Gibson coined the term "cyberspace" for "widespread, interconnected digital technology" in his short story "Burning Chrome" (1982), and later popularized the concept, along with his usage of the "matrix", in his acclaimed debut novel Neuromancer (1984). These early works of Gibson's have been credited with "renovating" science fiction literature in the 1980s.

title: Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom
author: Cory Doctorow
text: Published 2001. Genre: Science Fiction. In a future where death is obsolete and social status is paramount, Jules works at Disney World, striving to preserve its classic attractions. When a rival group threatens this artistic integrity by replacing beloved rides with immersive experiences, Jules finds himself killed and rebooted in a new body, igniting a conflict over the future of the park and the essence of creativity. Tone and style: satirical, fast-paced, humorous. Pacing: fast-paced, conflict-driven. Themes: identity, creativity, societal values. Setting: near-future Disney World in a post-scarcity society. About the author: Cory Efram Doctorow is a Canadian-British blogger, journalist, and science fiction author who served as co-editor of the blog Boing Boing. He is an activist in favour of liberalising copyright laws and a proponent of the Creative Commons organisation, using some of its licences for his books. Some common themes of his work include digital rights management, file sharing, and post-scarcity economics.

title: How to Do Nothing
author: Jenny Odell
text: Published 2019. Genre: Social Science. In "How to Do Nothing," Jenny Odell critiques the attention economy, arguing that our value is often dictated by productivity and constant connectivity. She advocates for reclaiming our attention as a vital resource, encouraging readers to engage in more meaningful political action and personal fulfillment outside of capitalist frameworks. The book serves as a guide to resisting societal pressures and rethinking our relationship with technology and nature. Tone and style: thoughtful, critical, engaging. Pacing: measured, reflective. Themes: attention economy, capitalism, personal agency. Setting: contemporary society and digital culture. About the author: Jenny Odell is an American multidisciplinary artist, writer, and educator based in Oakland, California. She taught Internet art and digital/physical design at Stanford University from 2013 to 2021. She wrote The New York Times best-selling book How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy (2019).

title: The Goldfinch
author: Donna Tart
text: Published 2013. Genre: Literary Fiction. The Goldfinch follows Theo Decker, a young boy who survives a tragic accident that kills his mother. As he navigates life in New York, he becomes entangled in the art world, driven by his attachment to a stolen painting that symbolizes his loss. The novel explores themes of grief, obsession, and the search for identity amidst chaos. Tone and style: introspective, lyrical, immersive. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: grief, obsession, identity, art. Setting: contemporary New York City. About the author: Donna Louise Tartt is an American novelist. She wrote the novels The Secret History (1992), The Little Friend (2002), and The Goldfinch (2013), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and was adapted into a 2019 film of the same name. She was included in Time magazine's 2014 "100 Most Influential People" list.

title: The Saint of Mt. Koya
author: Izumi Kyora
text: Published 1990. Genre: Literary Fiction. The Saint of Mt. Koya is a work by Japanese author Izumi Kyōka, exploring themes of spirituality and the human experience. The narrative likely delves into the significance of Mt. Koya, a sacred site in Japan, and its impact on the characters' lives. The book reflects on the intersection of faith and personal journeys. Tone and style: reflective, lyrical prose. Pacing: measured, contemplative. Themes: spirituality, self-discovery, nature. Setting: sacred Mt. Koya, Japan. About the author: Kyōtarō Izumi , known by his pen name Izumi Kyōka , was a Japanese novelist, writer and kabuki playwright who was active during the prewar period.

title: The Manager's Path
author: Camille Fournier
text: Published 2017. Genre: Business & Economics. The Manager's Path offers practical guidance for navigating the challenges of managing technical teams in the tech industry. Author Camille Fournier shares insights on transitioning from engineer to manager, mentoring, and fostering a positive team culture. The book addresses common pitfalls and provides strategies for effective leadership at various levels of management. Tone and style: practical, straightforward, informative. Pacing: structured, step-by-step. Themes: management, leadership, mentorship, team dynamics. Setting: tech industry management practices. About the author: Camille Fournier is known for being the former chief technology officer of Rent The Runway, former vice president of technology at Goldman Sachs, a former managing director at JPMorgan Chase, and author of The Manager's Path: A Guide for Tech Leaders Navigating Growth and Change. She is currently the VP Engineering of Common Services at CoreWeave.

title: Birding Without Borders
author: Noah Stryckland
text: Published 2017. Genre: Biography & Memoir. Noah Strycker recounts his journey to see half of the world's bird species in a single year, traveling through 41 countries. He shares the challenges he faced and the people he met, including fellow bird enthusiasts. The book captures the adventure and passion of birdwatching on a global scale. Tone and style: adventurous, engaging, informative. Pacing: fast-paced, travel-focused. Themes: exploration, nature, passion for birdwatching. Setting: global, spanning 41 countries. About the author: Noah Keefer Strycker is an American birdwatcher. In 2015, he set a record for a worldwide big year of birding, seeing 6,042 of the world's estimated 10,365 bird species at the time (58.3%), becoming the first person to record half of the world's birds in one year. His journey spanned 41 countries and all seven continents from January 1 to December 31, 2015.

title: Lean Analytics
author: Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz
text: Published 2013. Genre: Business & Economics. Lean Analytics provides a framework for startups to identify and measure key metrics that drive their business success. The book emphasizes the importance of data analysis in refining product offerings and achieving product/market fit. Through practical steps and case studies, it illustrates how entrepreneurs can leverage analytics to make informed decisions and iterate on their business models. Tone and style: practical, instructional, data-driven. Pacing: methodical, step-by-step. Themes: analytics, entrepreneurship, product development. Setting: startup ecosystem, technology sector.

title: Writers & Lovers
author: Lily King
text: Published 2020. Genre: Literary Fiction. Writers & Lovers follows Casey Peabody, a young woman grappling with the recent death of her mother and the fallout from a failed love affair. As she navigates life in Massachusetts in 1997, working as a waitress and struggling to complete her novel, Casey finds herself torn between two very different romantic interests. The novel explores her journey of artistic ambition, vulnerability, and the challenges of balancing personal desires with the demands of life. Tone and style: humorous, heartfelt, insightful. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: grief, creativity, love, ambition. Setting: 1997 Massachusetts, contemporary life. About the author: Lily King is an American novelist.

title: The Wise Man's Fear
author: Patrick Rothfuss
text: Published 2011. Genre: Fantasy. The Wise Man's Fear follows Kvothe as he navigates life outside the University, facing challenges in courtly politics and uncovering assassination plots. As he travels through Vintas, he confronts rival arcanists and leads mercenaries to solve mysteries surrounding the King's Road. The story delves into Kvothe's quest for knowledge about the Chandrian and the tragic past of his family. Tone and style: lyrical, immersive, character-driven. Pacing: measured, character-focused. Themes: identity, legend, revenge, knowledge. Setting: fantastical world with courtly society and wilderness. About the author: Patrick James Rothfuss is an American author. He is best known for his highly acclaimed series The Kingkiller Chronicle, beginning with Rothfuss' debut novel, The Name of the Wind (2007), which won several awards, and continuing in the sequel, The Wise Man's Fear (2011), which topped The New York Times Best Seller list.

title: Never Split the Difference
author: Christopher Voss
text: Published 2016. Genre: Business & Economics. Never Split the Difference is a negotiation guide based on the experiences of former FBI hostage negotiator Christopher Voss. It outlines effective negotiation techniques derived from high-stakes situations, demonstrating how these strategies can be applied in everyday life, from business dealings to personal relationships. Voss shares dramatic real-life scenarios to illustrate the principles of successful negotiation. Tone and style: practical, engaging, anecdotal. Pacing: direct, example-driven. Themes: negotiation, communication, strategy. Setting: various high-stakes negotiation scenarios. About the author: Christopher Voss is an American businessman, author, and academic. Voss is a former FBI hostage negotiator, the CEO of The Black Swan Group Ltd, a company registered in Las Vegas, Nevada, and co-author of the book Never Split the Difference. He is an adjunct professor at Harvard Law School and Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, and a lecturer at the Marshall School of Business at University of Southern California.

title: The Poppy War
author: R.F. Kuang
text: Published 2018. Genre: Fantasy. The Poppy War follows Rin, a dark-skinned war orphan from the poor, rural south of the Nikara Empire, who aces the Empire's competitive military academy. As she rises through the ranks, she discovers her shamanic powers and faces the brutal realities of war, including the impact of her actions on her country and her own identity. The novel explores themes of power, trauma, and the consequences of conflict, drawing inspiration from Chinese history. Tone and style: gritty, immersive, lyrical. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: war, identity, power, trauma. Setting: a fictional empire inspired by Chinese history. About the author: Rebecca F. Kuang is a Chinese-American novelist and short-story writer. She is known for her fantasy novels, which includes The Poppy War trilogy and her 2022 novel Babel, or the Necessity of Violence, which placed first on The New York Times Best Seller list and won the 2022 Nebula Award for Best Novel. She is currently the inaugural Millard Distinguished Writer in Residence at the College of the Holy Cross.

title: The Killing Floor (Jack Reacher)
author: Lee Child
text: Published 2012-11-06. Genre: Thriller. Jack Reacher, a former military policeman, finds himself in the small town of Margrave, Georgia, where he is wrongfully arrested for murder shortly after his arrival. As he seeks to clear his name, he uncovers a web of corruption and crime within the town. The story follows Reacher as he navigates the challenges of proving his innocence while dealing with local law enforcement and uncovering deeper conspiracies. Tone and style: gritty, suspenseful, straightforward. Pacing: fast-paced, action-driven. Themes: justice, corruption, survival. Setting: contemporary small-town Georgia. About the author: James Dover Grant, primarily known by his pen name Lee Child, is a British author who writes thriller novels and is best known for his Jack Reacher novel series. The books follow the adventures of a former American military policeman, Jack Reacher, who wanders the United States. His first novel, Killing Floor (1997), won the Anthony Award and the 1998 Barry Award for Best First Novel.

title: I Like to Watch
author: Emily Nussbaum
text: Published 2019. Genre: Other. Emily Nussbaum's collection of essays examines the cultural significance of television and its impact on society. She discusses various aspects of TV, including the portrayal of female characters, the influence of fans, and the complexities of artistic integrity in the context of problematic creators. Through her critiques, Nussbaum advocates for a broader appreciation of television as a legitimate art form, challenging the conventional hierarchies of cultural value. Tone and style: insightful, engaging, humorous. Pacing: varied, reflective. Themes: television criticism, cultural identity, artistic integrity. Setting: contemporary American television landscape. About the author: Emily Nussbaum is an American critic and arts journalist. She is the theater critic for The New Yorker, where she was television critic from 2011 until 2019. In 2016, she won the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism.

title: There There
author: Tommy Orange
text: Published 2018. Genre: Literary Fiction. There There follows the interconnected lives of several Native American characters living in Oakland, California, as they prepare for a powwow. Each character grapples with their identity, personal struggles, and the legacy of their heritage. The novel explores themes of violence, recovery, and the complexities of modern Native American life. Tone and style: raw, poignant, multi-voiced. Pacing: fast-paced, interwoven narratives. Themes: identity, violence, recovery, community, dislocation. Setting: contemporary Oakland, California. About the author: Tommy Orange is an American novelist and writer from Oakland, California. His first book, There There (2018), was a finalist for the 2019 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and received the 2019 American Book Award. In October 2025, Orange was awarded a MacArthur Foundation Fellowship.

title: Harlem Shuffle
author: Colson Whitehead
text: Published 2021. Genre: Literary Fiction. Harlem Shuffle follows Ray Carney, a furniture salesman in 1960s Harlem, who struggles to balance his respectable life with his family's criminal past. When his cousin Freddie involves him in a robbery scheme, Ray is drawn deeper into the underworld of Harlem's crime scene. The novel explores themes of race, power, and morality as Ray navigates his dual identity amidst the vibrant backdrop of Harlem. Tone and style: witty, engaging, richly detailed. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: race, identity, morality, family. Setting: Harlem, New York City in the early 1960s. About the author: Arch Colson Chipp Whitehead is an American novelist. He is the author of ten novels, including his 1999 debut The Intuitionist; The Underground Railroad (2016), for which he won the 2016 National Book Award for Fiction and the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; and The Nickel Boys, for which he won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction again in 2020, making him one of only four writers ever to win the prize twice. He has also published two books of nonfiction. In 2002, he received a MacArthur Fellowship.

title: Freedom
author: Jonathan Franzen
text: Published 2010-08-31. Genre: Literary Fiction. Freedom follows the lives of Patty and Walter Berglund, a seemingly perfect couple living in St. Paul, as they navigate the complexities of marriage, parenthood, and societal expectations. As their teenage son moves in with a politically opposite family and Walter takes a controversial job, the story explores themes of personal freedom, compromise, and the impact of suburban life. The novel delves into the characters' struggles with love, ambition, and the changing dynamics of their relationships. Tone and style: wry, introspective, character-driven. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: love, marriage, freedom, suburban life, compromise. Setting: contemporary suburban America. About the author: Jonathan Earl Franzen is an American novelist and essayist. His 2001 novel The Corrections drew widespread critical acclaim, earned Franzen a National Book Award, was a Pulitzer Prize for Fiction finalist, earned a James Tait Black Memorial Prize, and was shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Award. His novel Freedom (2010) garnered similar praise and led to an appearance on the cover of Time magazine alongside the headline "Great American Novelist". Franzen's latest novel Crossroads was published in 2021, and is the first in a projected trilogy.

title: The Spy who Came In From The Cold
author: John La Carre
text:
Published 1962. Genre: Espionage/Spy. In the midst of the Cold War, British spy Alec Leamas is drawn into one last dangerous mission against the East German Secret Service. As he navigates a world of espionage filled with deception, he finds himself falling in love, complicating his role in a ruthless game of betrayal. The novel explores the tension between personal relationships and the morally ambiguous nature of spy work. Tone and style: dark, tense, morally complex. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: betrayal, love, moral ambiguity. Setting: Cold War Europe. About the author: David John Moore Cornwell, known by his pen name John le Carré, was an English author. 
Many of his espionage novels have been adapted for film or television. He has been described as a "sophisticated, morally ambiguous writer", and is considered one of the greatest novelists of the postwar era. During the 1950s and 1960s, he worked for both the Security Service (MI5) and the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6). Near the end of his life, le Carré became an Irish citizen.

title: Birnam Wood
author: Eleanor Catton
text: Published 2023. Genre: Literary Fiction. Birnam Wood follows a guerrilla gardening collective in New Zealand as they seek to occupy an abandoned farm after a landslide. The group's founder, Mira, encounters an American billionaire who offers them a deal that could secure their future, but trust becomes a central issue as their intentions and ideologies clash. The novel explores themes of ambition, greed, and the unforeseen consequences of well-meaning actions. Tone and style: witty, dramatic, introspective. Pacing: tension-filled, character-driven. Themes: ambition, trust, environmentalism, survival. Setting: contemporary New Zealand. About the author: Eleanor Catton is a New Zealand novelist and screenwriter. Born in Canada, Catton moved to New Zealand as a child and grew up in Christchurch. She completed a master's degree in creative writing at the International Institute of Modern Letters. Her award-winning debut novel, The Rehearsal, written as her Master's thesis, was published in 2008, and has been adapted into a 2016 film of the same name. Her second novel, The Luminaries, won the 2013 Booker Prize, making Catton the youngest author ever to win the prize and only the second New Zealander. It was subsequently adapted into a television miniseries, with Catton as screenwriter. In 2023, she was named on the Granta Best of Young British Novelists list.

title: No Bad Kids: Toddler Discipline without Shame
author: Janet Lansbury
text: Published 2014. Genre: Self-Help & Personal Development. No Bad Kids offers practical strategies for parents to discipline toddlers while maintaining a respectful relationship. Janet Lansbury draws on her extensive experience in child care to address common toddler behaviors and provide guidance on setting boundaries without resorting to yelling. The book emphasizes the importance of compassion and love in discipline, making it a valuable resource for parents navigating the challenges of toddlerhood. Tone and style: practical, compassionate, encouraging. Pacing: measured, advice-driven. Themes: discipline, respect, toddler behavior. Setting: contemporary parenting context. About the author: Janet Lansbury is an American educator and former actress, credited as Janet Julian for much of her career.

title: Chip Wars
author: Chris Miller
text: Published 2022. Genre: History. Chip Wars explores the geopolitical and economic significance of microchip technology, likening its importance to that of oil. The book details the historical rise of the United States in chip design and manufacturing, the challenges posed by China’s ambitions in the semiconductor industry, and the implications for military and economic power in the modern world. Tone and style: analytical, engaging, informative. Pacing: methodical, detailed. Themes: geopolitics, technology, economic competition. Setting: modern global landscape, U.S. and China. About the author: Chris or Christopher Miller may refer to:

title: Circe
author: Margaret Miller
text: Published 2018. Genre: Fantasy. Circe, the daughter of Helios, struggles with her identity and power in a world dominated by gods and mortals. Isolated on a remote island after being exiled by Zeus, she hones her skills as a witch and encounters various legendary figures from mythology. As she faces threats from both gods and humans, Circe must choose between her divine heritage and her love for humanity. Tone and style: lyrical, introspective, mythic. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: identity, power, isolation, love. Setting: ancient Greece and mythological realms. About the author: Madeline Miller is an American novelist, author of The Song of Achilles (2011) and Circe (2018). Miller spent ten years writing The Song of Achilles while she worked as a teacher of Latin and Greek. The novel tells the story of the love between the mythological figures Achilles and Patroclus; it won the Orange Prize for Fiction, making Miller the fourth debut novelist to win the prize. She is a 2019 recipient of the Alex Awards.

title: Prep
author: Curtis Sittenfeld
text: Published 2005. Genre: Literary Fiction. Lee Fiora, a fourteen-year-old scholarship student, navigates the complexities of life at the prestigious Ault School in Massachusetts. As she observes and engages with her affluent peers, she grapples with feelings of alienation and belonging. Her journey through adolescence is marked by intense friendships, a complicated crush, and the challenges of maintaining her identity in a world that often feels foreign to her. Tone and style: observant, introspective, nuanced. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: adolescence, social class, identity, belonging. Setting: prestigious Massachusetts prep school. About the author: Elizabeth Curtis Sittenfeld is an American writer. She is the author of two collections of short stories, You Think it, I’ll Say It (2018) and Show Don't Tell (2025), as well as seven novels: Prep (2005), the story of students at a Massachusetts prep school; The Man of My Dreams (2006), a coming-of-age novel and an examination of romantic love; American Wife (2008), a fictional story loosely based on the life of First Lady Laura Bush; Sisterland (2013), which tells the story of identical twins with psychic powers; Eligible (2016), a modern-day retelling of Pride and Prejudice; Rodham (2020), an alternate history political novel about the life of Hillary Clinton; and Romantic Comedy (2023), a romance between a comedy writer and a pop star.

title: Romantic Comedy
author: Curtis Sittenfeld
text: Published 2023. Genre: Romance. Sally Milz, a sketch writer for a late-night comedy show, has given up on love after a series of heartbreaks. However, her life takes a turn when she meets Noah Brewster, a pop star known for dating models, while working on a show together. As they collaborate, Sally begins to question her assumptions about romance and whether someone like Noah could ever be interested in her. Tone and style: witty, contemporary, insightful. Pacing: steady, character-driven. Themes: love, gender dynamics, self-discovery. Setting: modern-day comedy scene in the US. About the author: Elizabeth Curtis Sittenfeld is an American writer. She is the author of two collections of short stories, You Think it, I’ll Say It (2018) and Show Don't Tell (2025), as well as seven novels: Prep (2005), the story of students at a Massachusetts prep school; The Man of My Dreams (2006), a coming-of-age novel and an examination of romantic love; American Wife (2008), a fictional story loosely based on the life of First Lady Laura Bush; Sisterland (2013), which tells the story of identical twins with psychic powers; Eligible (2016), a modern-day retelling of Pride and Prejudice; Rodham (2020), an alternate history political novel about the life of Hillary Clinton; and Romantic Comedy (2023), a romance between a comedy writer and a pop star.

title: Gideon the Ninth
author: Tamsyn Muir
text: Published 2019. Genre: Science Fiction. Gideon the Ninth follows Gideon, a swordswoman raised by the Ninth House's necromancers, as she seeks to escape her life of servitude. When her childhood rival, Harrowhark, needs her assistance to compete in a deadly trial set by the Emperor, the two must navigate a treacherous competition filled with political intrigue and supernatural challenges. The story blends elements of science fiction and fantasy, featuring necromancy and a unique gothic setting in space. Tone and style: darkly humorous, immersive. Pacing: fast-paced, plot-driven. Themes: identity, power dynamics, loyalty. Setting: a gothic palace in a solar system. About the author: Tamsyn Elizabeth Muir is a New Zealand fantasy, science fiction, and horror author best known for The Locked Tomb, a science fantasy series of novels. Muir won the 2020 Locus Award for her first novel, Gideon the Ninth, and has been nominated for several other awards as well.

title: Convenience Store Woman
author: Sayaka Murata
text: Published 2018. Genre: Literary Fiction. Convenience Store Woman follows Keiko Furukura, a 36-year-old woman who finds her place in the world working at a convenience store in Tokyo. Despite her contentment in this role, societal pressures from her family and peers push her to conform to traditional expectations of marriage and career. The novel explores themes of individuality, societal norms, and the complexities of modern work culture through Keiko's unique perspective. Tone and style: ironic, sharp-eyed, introspective. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: identity, conformity, societal pressure. Setting: contemporary Tokyo, Japan. About the author: Sayaka Murata is a Japanese writer. She is best known for the international bestseller Convenience Store Woman (2016) which has been translated into more than thirty languages worldwide. Murata has won many major literary prizes in Japan, including the Gunzo Prize for New Writers in 2003, the Noma Literary New Face Prize in 2009, the Mishima Yukio Prize in 2013, and the Akutagawa Prize for Convenience Store Woman in 2016. All the English translations of her work are done by Ginny Tapley Takemori. In addition to Convenience Store Woman, Murata's first book to be published in English, Takemori has translated the novels Earthlings and Vanishing World, the short-story collection Life Ceremony, the short stories "Faith", "Survival", and "A Clean Marriage", as well as the New York Times published opinion piece "The Future of Sex Lives in All of Us", among others.

title: Making Number Counts
author: Chip Heath
text: Published 2022. Genre: Business & Economics. Making Numbers Count offers practical strategies for effectively communicating and understanding complex numerical data. Chip Heath explores how to translate abstract numbers into relatable concepts, using vivid comparisons and emotional framing to enhance comprehension. The book provides principles and examples that help readers grasp the significance of numbers in everyday contexts, making data more accessible and impactful. Tone and style: clear, practical, engaging. Pacing: methodical, example-driven. Themes: communication, data visualization, understanding numbers. Setting: contemporary applications in various fields. About the author: Chip Heath is an American academic. He is the Thrive Foundation for Youth Professor of Organizational Behavior at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, and the co-author of several books.

title: Demon Copperhead
author: Barbara Kingsolver
text: Published 2022. Genre: Literary Fiction. Demon Copperhead follows a boy born to a teenage single mother in southern Appalachia, navigating the challenges of foster care, child labor, and addiction. Through his unsparing voice, he confronts the invisibility of rural people in modern culture while reflecting on the enduring issues of poverty and loss. This contemporary retelling of Dickens' David Copperfield explores the transformative power of storytelling amidst the struggles of a new generation. Tone and style: raw, poignant, reflective. Pacing: character-driven, episodic. Themes: poverty, resilience, identity, loss. Setting: contemporary southern Appalachia. About the author: Barbara Ellen Kingsolver is an American novelist, essayist, and poet. Her widely known works include The Poisonwood Bible, the tale of a missionary family in the Congo; and Animal, Vegetable, Miracle, a nonfiction account of her family's attempts to eat locally. In 2023, she was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for the novel Demon Copperhead. Her work often focuses on topics such as social justice, biodiversity, and the interaction between humans and their communities and environments.

title: Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy
author: John le Carre
text:
Published 1974. Genre: Espionage/Spy. George Smiley, a seasoned intelligence officer, is tasked with uncovering a Soviet mole within the British Secret Service during the Cold War. The narrative delves into themes of betrayal and loyalty, as Smiley navigates a web of deception and moral ambiguity. The story is marked by its intricate plotting and character-driven tension. Tone and style: sophisticated, morally ambiguous. Pacing: deliberate, suspenseful. Themes: betrayal, loyalty, moral ambiguity. Setting: Cold War Britain. About the author: David John Moore Cornwell, known by his pen name John le Carré, was an English author. 
Many of his espionage novels have been adapted for film or television. He has been described as a "sophisticated, morally ambiguous writer", and is considered one of the greatest novelists of the postwar era. During the 1950s and 1960s, he worked for both the Security Service (MI5) and the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6). Near the end of his life, le Carré became an Irish citizen.

title: Superpumped
author: Mike Isaac
text: Published 2022. Genre: Business & Economics. Superpumped details the rise and fall of Uber, focusing on its founder Travis Kalanick and the company's aggressive business practices. It explores how Uber disrupted the taxi industry while engaging in unethical behavior, including spying, bribery, and fostering a toxic corporate culture. The book serves as a cautionary tale about the consequences of unchecked ambition and corporate greed in Silicon Valley. Tone and style: engaging, investigative, critical. Pacing: fast-paced, narrative-driven. Themes: corporate ethics, ambition, disruption, technology culture. Setting: Silicon Valley and the global transportation industry. About the author: Super Pumped: The Battle for Uber is a 2019 book by New York Times journalist Mike Isaac. The book covers the events between the founding of Uber and its initial public offering in 2019.

title: The Honourable Schoolboy
author: John le Carre
text:
Published 1977. Genre: Espionage/Spy. In 'The Honourable Schoolboy', George Smiley, a key figure in British intelligence, seeks to restore his espionage network after a betrayal. He assigns one of his most trusted agents to navigate the complex political landscape of the Far East, where he confronts both external threats and internal challenges within the intelligence community. Tone and style: sophisticated, morally complex. Pacing: deliberate, character-driven. Themes: betrayal, loyalty, espionage. Setting: Cold War-era Far East. About the author: David John Moore Cornwell, known by his pen name John le Carré, was an English author. 
Many of his espionage novels have been adapted for film or television. He has been described as a "sophisticated, morally ambiguous writer", and is considered one of the greatest novelists of the postwar era. During the 1950s and 1960s, he worked for both the Security Service (MI5) and the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6). Near the end of his life, le Carré became an Irish citizen.

title: A Psalm for the Wild-Built
author: Becky Chambers
text: Published 2021. Genre: Science Fiction. A Psalm for the Wild-Built follows a tea monk and a robot in a post-human world where robots have gained self-awareness and retreated into the wilderness. The story explores the monk's encounter with the robot, who seeks to understand human needs and the meaning of fulfillment in a society that has achieved its desires. Through their conversations, the book delves into themes of purpose, connection, and what it means to live a meaningful life. Tone and style: thoughtful, conversational, introspective. Pacing: measured, reflective. Themes: identity, purpose, connection. Setting: post-human future, wilderness. About the author: Becky Chambers is an American science fiction writer. She is the author of the Hugo Award-winning Wayfarers series as well as novellas including To Be Taught, If Fortunate (2019) and the Monk & Robot series, which begins with the Hugo Award-winning A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021). She is known for her innovative worldbuilding and character-driven stories, and is a pioneer of the hopepunk genre.

title: A Prayer for the Crown-shy
author: Becky Chambers
text: Published 2022. Genre: Science Fiction. A Prayer for the Crown-shy follows Sibling Dex, a Tea Monk, and Mosscap, a robot, as they explore the villages and cities of their moon, seeking to understand humanity's needs. Their journey is marked by encounters that emphasize kindness, friendship, and the exploration of what truly matters in life. The story continues to delve into themes of fulfillment and the nature of existence in a world where desires are met. Tone and style: gentle, introspective, hopeful. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: kindness, fulfillment, human connection. Setting: rural and urban areas of a fictional moon. About the author: Becky Chambers is an American science fiction writer. She is the author of the Hugo Award-winning Wayfarers series as well as novellas including To Be Taught, If Fortunate (2019) and the Monk & Robot series, which begins with the Hugo Award-winning A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021). She is known for her innovative worldbuilding and character-driven stories, and is a pioneer of the hopepunk genre.

title: Sharks in the Time of Saviors
author: Kawai Strong Washburn
text: Published 2020. Genre: Literary Fiction. Sharks in the Time of Saviors follows the Flores family in Hawaii after a young boy, Nainoa, is rescued by a shark during a family vacation. This miraculous event leads the family to believe he has been favored by Hawaiian gods, but as Nainoa grows up, his supernatural abilities create tension and division among family members. Each sibling grapples with their identity and heritage as they navigate personal struggles and the impact of their shared past. Tone and style: lyrical, emotional, introspective. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: family, heritage, identity, supernatural. Setting: 1990s Hawaii and contemporary Pacific Northwest. About the author: Kawai Strong Washburn is an American writer and novelist, best known for his debut novel Sharks in the Time of Saviors (2020) which won the Hemingway Foundation/PEN Award and the Minnesota Book Award in 2021.

title: To Be Taught, If Fortunate
author: Becky Chambers
text: Published 2019. Genre: Science Fiction. In the twenty-second century, astronauts can transform their bodies through a process called somaforming, allowing them to survive in hostile environments on distant exoplanets. Ariadne, one of these explorers, chronicles her journey as she ecologically surveys four habitable worlds while grappling with the changes back on Earth. As she and her crewmates adapt physically and mentally, they confront the challenges of returning to a world that may have forgotten them. Tone and style: thoughtful, introspective, lyrical. Pacing: measured, reflective. Themes: exploration, identity, change. Setting: distant exoplanets and a transformed Earth. About the author: Becky Chambers is an American science fiction writer. She is the author of the Hugo Award-winning Wayfarers series as well as novellas including To Be Taught, If Fortunate (2019) and the Monk & Robot series, which begins with the Hugo Award-winning A Psalm for the Wild-Built (2021). She is known for her innovative worldbuilding and character-driven stories, and is a pioneer of the hopepunk genre.

title: Light from Uncommon Stars
author: Ryka Aoki
text: Published 2021. Genre: Science Fiction. Light from Uncommon Stars follows Shizuka Satomi, a violinist who has made a Faustian bargain to save her soul by luring seven prodigies into similar deals. When she discovers Katrina Nguyen, a talented transgender runaway, she believes she has found her final candidate. Their lives intersect with Lan Tran, a retired starship captain, leading to a story that intertwines themes of magic, identity, and the power of family. Tone and style: joyful, whimsical, heartfelt. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: identity, magic, family, hope, curses. Setting: California's San Gabriel Valley, contemporary. About the author: Ryka Aoki is an American author of novels, poetry, and essays. She teaches English at Santa Monica College and gender studies at Antioch University.

title: Strangers on a Train
author: Patricia Highsmith
text: Published 1950. Genre: Thriller. Strangers on a Train follows Guy Haines, a successful architect, who meets the enigmatic Charles Bruno on a train. Bruno proposes a chilling idea of swapping murders to solve their respective problems, leading Guy into a web of manipulation and psychological turmoil as he struggles to extricate himself from Bruno's increasingly dangerous obsession. Tone and style: tense, psychological, suspenseful. Pacing: fast-paced, plot-driven. Themes: morality, obsession, identity. Setting: mid-20th century America. About the author: Patricia Highsmith was an American novelist and short story writer widely known for her psychological thrillers, including her series of five novels featuring the character Tom Ripley. She wrote 22 novels and numerous short stories in a career spanning nearly five decades, and her work has led to more than two dozen film adaptations. Her writing was influenced by existentialist literature and questioned notions of identity and popular morality. She was dubbed "the poet of apprehension" by novelist Graham Greene.

title: Kitchen Confidential
author: Anthony Bourdain
text: Published 2000. Genre: Biography & Memoir. In 'Kitchen Confidential', Anthony Bourdain shares his candid experiences as a chef in New York City, detailing the gritty realities of the restaurant industry. He discusses the challenges of drug use, sexual encounters, and the often harsh dynamics within kitchen environments. The book serves as both a memoir and an exposé of the culinary world. Tone and style: raw, candid, humorous. Pacing: fast-paced, anecdotal. Themes: addiction, ambition, culinary culture. Setting: New York City restaurant scene. About the author: Anthony Michael Bourdain was an American celebrity chef, author, and travel documentarian. He starred in programs focusing on the exploration of international culture, cuisine, and the human condition.

title: Too Like the Lightning
author: Ada Palmer
text: Published 2016. Genre: Science Fiction. In a future utopia of the 25th century, Mycroft Canner, a convict, must navigate a society that has outlawed public religion and enforces strict social norms around gender. He encounters Carlyle Foster, a spiritual counselor, and together they grapple with the implications of a boy named Bridger, who possesses the ability to make his wishes come true, potentially threatening the stability of their world. Tone and style: thought-provoking, intricate prose. Pacing: slow-burn, philosophical exploration. Themes: utopia, identity, societal norms, power. Setting: 25th-century human society. About the author: Ada Palmer is an American historian and writer. She is an associate professor at the University of Chicago and wrote the science fiction series Terra Ignota. The first novel in the series, Too Like the Lightning, was published in May 2016. The work has been well received by critics and was a finalist for the Hugo Award for Best Novel. She received the 2017 John W. Campbell Award for Best New Writer.

title: Seven Surrenders
author: Ada Palmer
text: Published 2017. Genre: Science Fiction. In a future characterized by instantaneous global travel and a history devoid of war, the stability of society is threatened by hidden conspiracies among the leaders of the Hives, who manipulate events through calculated murders. Mycroft Canner, a convict serving the world, and Carlyle Foster, a counselor with burdensome secrets, are both aware of a child named Bridger, who possesses the ability to animate inanimate objects, which could disrupt the fragile balance of power. This novel explores themes of love, murder, and high politics within a richly constructed science fiction world. Tone and style: wry, erudite, inventive. Pacing: fast-paced, idea-driven. Themes: conspiracy, power dynamics, morality, identity. Setting: futuristic society with global travel. About the author: Ada Palmer is an American historian and writer. She is an associate professor at the University of Chicago and wrote the science fiction series Terra Ignota. The first novel in the series, Too Like the Lightning, was published in May 2016. The work has been well received by critics and was a finalist for the Hugo Award for Best Novel. She received the 2017 John W. Campbell Award for Best New Writer.

title: The Magicians
author: Lev Grossman
text: Published 2009. Genre: Fantasy. Quentin Coldwater, a high school math genius, is admitted to a secret college of magic, fulfilling his childhood dreams of escaping to a fantastical world. However, his experiences reveal the dark and dangerous realities of magic and the fantasy land of Fillory, leading him to confront disillusionment and the consequences of his desires. The novel explores themes of coming-of-age and the complexities of fantasy versus reality. Tone and style: dark, introspective, lyrical. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: disillusionment, coming-of-age, the nature of fantasy. Setting: modern-day New York and a magical college. About the author: Lev Grossman is an American novelist and journalist who wrote the Magicians trilogy: The Magicians (2009), The Magician King (2011), and The Magician's Land (2014). He was the book critic and lead technology writer at Time magazine from 2002 to 2016. His recent work includes the children's book The Silver Arrow and its sequel, The Golden Swift; The Bright Sword, a reimagining of the King Arthur legend; and the screenplay for the film The Map of Tiny Perfect Things, based on his short story.

title: The Lumumba Plot
author: Stuart A. Reid
text: Published 2023. Genre: History. The Lumumba Plot explores the U.S.-backed conspiracy to assassinate Patrice Lumumba, the first democratically elected Prime Minister of the Congo, shortly after the country gained independence in 1960. The narrative details the political chaos that ensued, including Lumumba's appeal to the Soviets for help, the CIA's involvement in his removal, and the subsequent rise of Joseph Mobutu. This historical account highlights the broader implications of U.S. foreign intervention during the Cold War. Tone and style: engaging, detailed, investigative. Pacing: methodical, unfolding narrative. Themes: colonialism, political intrigue, Cold War. Setting: 1960s Congo and U.S. political landscape.

title: The Singapore Story
author: Lee Kuan Yew
text: Published 1998. Genre: Biography & Memoir. The Singapore Story is the first volume of Lee Kuan Yew's memoirs, detailing his role in Singapore's journey to independence. He recounts his political battles against colonialism, communism, and communalism, highlighting key alliances and conflicts that shaped the nation. The memoir offers insights into his strategies and the political landscape of Singapore during his leadership. Tone and style: detailed, candid, reflective. Pacing: chronological, anecdotal. Themes: leadership, independence, political struggle. Setting: 20th-century Singapore and its political landscape. About the author: Lee Kuan Yew, also known as LKY, was a Singaporean politician and barrister who served as the first prime minister of Singapore from 1959 to 1990. A member of the People's Action Party (PAP), his authoritarian governance oversaw the transformation of post-independence Singapore into a highly developed country and one of the four Asian Tigers. He is regarded as the founding father of modern Singapore.

title: Nickel Boys
author: Colson Whitehead
text: Published 2019. Genre: Literary Fiction. The Nickel Boys follows the harrowing experiences of Elwood Curtis, a young black boy sentenced to a brutal reform school in 1960s Florida. The story explores his friendship with Turner, who is skeptical of Elwood's optimistic ideals in the face of the school's horrors. Their contrasting perspectives on survival and justice lead to a pivotal decision with lasting consequences, reflecting the grim realities of racial injustice in America. Tone and style: gritty, poignant, evocative. Pacing: intense, character-driven. Themes: friendship, racial injustice, survival, hope. Setting: Jim Crow-era Florida. About the author: Arch Colson Chipp Whitehead is an American novelist. He is the author of ten novels, including his 1999 debut The Intuitionist; The Underground Railroad (2016), for which he won the 2016 National Book Award for Fiction and the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; and The Nickel Boys, for which he won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction again in 2020, making him one of only four writers ever to win the prize twice. He has also published two books of nonfiction. In 2002, he received a MacArthur Fellowship.

title: Vanishing Treasures
author: Katherine Rundell
text: Published 2024. Genre: Other. In "Vanishing Treasures," Katherine Rundell explores the fascinating lives of 23 endangered animals, highlighting their unique behaviors and the urgent need for conservation. Through a series of essays, she aims to rekindle a sense of wonder about the natural world and the creatures that inhabit it. The book serves as both a celebration of these extraordinary beings and a call to action to protect their fragile existence. Tone and style: insightful, passionate, witty. Pacing: reflective, essay-driven. Themes: endangerment, conservation, wonder of nature. Setting: global, focusing on endangered species. About the author: Katherine Rundell is an English author and academic. She is the author of Impossible Creatures, named Waterstones Book of the Year for 2023. She is also the author of Rooftoppers, which in 2015 won both the overall Waterstones Children's Book Prize and the Blue Peter Book Award for Best Story, and was shortlisted for the Carnegie Medal. She is a Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford and has appeared as an expert guest on BBC Radio 4 programmes including Start the Week, Poetry Please,  Seriously.... and Private Passions.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
text: Published 2016. Genre: Self-Help & Personal Development. Atomic Habits explores the power of small, incremental changes in behavior to achieve significant personal transformation. James Clear argues that by focusing on tiny habits, such as waking up slightly earlier or engaging in brief exercise routines, individuals can create lasting improvements in their lives. The book combines scientific explanations with motivational stories of successful individuals to illustrate how these small changes can lead to remarkable results. Tone and style: practical, motivational, accessible. Pacing: methodical, evidence-based. Themes: habits, personal growth, behavior change. Setting: contemporary self-improvement context. About the author: James Clear is an American writer. Raised in Hamilton, Ohio, and receiving education from Denison University and Ohio State University, he is best known for his 2018 self-help book Atomic Habits.

title: Crazy Rich Asians
author: Kevin Kwan
text: Published 2013. Genre: Literary Fiction. Crazy Rich Asians follows Rachel Chu, an American-born Chinese woman, as she travels to Singapore with her wealthy boyfriend, Nicholas Young, for a wedding. Unbeknownst to her, Nick's family is part of the ultra-rich elite, leading to a summer filled with opulence, social tensions, and family drama. The novel explores themes of class, identity, and cultural expectations within the context of Asian high society. Tone and style: witty, satirical, vibrant. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: wealth, identity, family dynamics, cultural clash. Setting: contemporary Singapore among the wealthy elite. About the author: Kevin Kwan is a Singaporean-born American novelist and writer of satirical novels Crazy Rich Asians, China Rich Girlfriend, and Rich People Problems. His latest book, Lies and Weddings, was released in June 2024.

title: All Systems Red
author: Martha Wells
text: Published 2017. Genre: Science Fiction. In a corporate-controlled future, a self-aware security android known as Murderbot has hacked its own governor module and prefers to avoid human interaction. Tasked with protecting a group of scientists on a distant planet, it grapples with its identity while uncovering the truth behind a neighboring mission that has gone silent. The story explores themes of consciousness and autonomy in the context of artificial intelligence. Tone and style: wry, introspective, accessible. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: identity, autonomy, artificial intelligence. Setting: distant planet in a corporate spacefaring future. About the author: Martha Wells is an American writer of speculative fiction. She has published a number of science fiction and fantasy (SF/F) novels, young adult novels, media tie-ins, short stories, and nonfiction essays on SF/F subjects. Her novels have been translated into twelve languages. Wells credits her academic background in anthropology for her interest in designing complex, realistically detailed societies within her novels.

title: The Quiet American
author: Graham Greene
text: Published 1940. Genre: Literary Fiction. The Quiet American follows Fowler, a cynical British journalist in Vietnam, as he navigates the complexities of war and politics. He becomes entangled with Pyle, an idealistic American who believes in promoting democracy through a 'Third Force.' As Pyle's actions lead to unintended violence, Fowler grapples with his own motivations and moral dilemmas, questioning the impact of foreign intervention. Tone and style: cynical, reflective, poignant. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: idealism, colonialism, moral ambiguity. Setting: 1950s Vietnam during the French Indochina War. About the author: Henry Graham Greene was an English writer and journalist regarded by many as one of the leading novelists of the 20th century.

title: The Mountain in the Sea
author: Ray Nayler
text: Published 2022. Genre: Science Fiction. In a near-future setting, a marine biologist named Dr. Ha Nguyen investigates a newly discovered species of intelligent octopus with its own language and culture on the Con Dao Archipelago. As she works with a team from the tech corporation DIANIMA, they face competition from various forces seeking to exploit the octopuses for their own ends. The story explores themes of consciousness and the ecological implications of human intervention. Tone and style: thought-provoking, lyrical prose. Pacing: tension-filled, character-driven. Themes: intelligence, ecology, communication, corporate greed. Setting: near-future Con Dao Archipelago. About the author: Ray Nayler is an American and Canadian writer whose works engage with ecology, systems theory, and questions of consciousness and intelligence, including animal and artificial intelligence.

title: Crook Manifesto
author: Colson Whitehead
text: Published 2023. Genre: Literary Fiction. Set in 1970s New York, 'Crook Manifesto' follows Ray Carney, a furniture store owner and former fence, as he navigates the chaotic streets of Harlem. As crime rises and the city faces bankruptcy, Carney's attempts to lead a straight life are complicated by his past connections and the violent antics of his partner, Pepper. The novel explores themes of family and survival against the backdrop of a city in turmoil, blending dark humor with a vivid portrayal of the era. Tone and style: darkly funny, vivid prose. Pacing: fast-paced, character-driven. Themes: crime, family, survival, urban decay. Setting: 1970s Harlem, New York City. About the author: Arch Colson Chipp Whitehead is an American novelist. He is the author of ten novels, including his 1999 debut The Intuitionist; The Underground Railroad (2016), for which he won the 2016 National Book Award for Fiction and the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction; and The Nickel Boys, for which he won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction again in 2020, making him one of only four writers ever to win the prize twice. He has also published two books of nonfiction. In 2002, he received a MacArthur Fellowship.

title: Brideshead Revisited
author: Evelyn Waugh
text: Published 1945. Genre: Literary Fiction. Brideshead Revisited follows Charles Ryder as he reflects on his relationships with the aristocratic Flyte family, particularly Sebastian and Julia. Set against the backdrop of England between the two World Wars, the novel explores themes of faith, love, and the decline of the British aristocracy, while delving into the complexities of sin and redemption. Tone and style: elegant, introspective, nostalgic. Pacing: measured, reflective. Themes: faith, love, aristocracy, decline. Setting: England between the two World Wars. About the author: Arthur Evelyn St. John Waugh was an English writer of novels, biographies, and travel books; he was also a prolific journalist and book reviewer. His most famous works include the early satires Decline and Fall (1928) and A Handful of Dust (1934), the novel Brideshead Revisited (1945), and the Second World War trilogy Sword of Honour (1952–1961). He is recognised as one of the great prose stylists of the English language in the 20th century.

title: The Wild Robot
author: Peter Brown
text: Published 2016. Genre: Children's Fiction. Roz the robot finds herself stranded on a remote island with no recollection of her past. To survive, she must adapt to her new surroundings and learn from the island's various creatures, some of whom are initially hostile. The story explores themes of nature, friendship, and self-discovery. Tone and style: whimsical, engaging, accessible. Pacing: steady, character-focused. Themes: survival, adaptation, friendship, nature. Setting: a remote, wild island. About the author: Peter Brown may refer to:

title: Down and Out in Paris and London
author: George Orwell
text: Published 1933. Genre: Biography & Memoir. In "Down and Out in Paris and London," George Orwell provides a firsthand account of his experiences with poverty in both cities. The narrative reveals the struggles of the destitute and critiques the socio-economic conditions of the early 20th century. Through vivid observations and a blend of memoir and social commentary, Orwell highlights the harsh realities faced by those living on the margins of society. Tone and style: poignant, satirical, observational. Pacing: reflective, immersive. Themes: poverty, social injustice, economic disparity. Setting: early 20th-century Paris and London. About the author: Eric Arthur Blair was an English novelist, poet, essayist, journalist, and critic who wrote under the pen name of George Orwell. His work is characterised by lucid prose, social criticism, opposition to all totalitarianism, and support of democratic socialism.

title: Normal People
author: Sally Rooney
text: Published 2018. Genre: Literary Fiction. Normal People follows the complex relationship between Connell and Marianne, two teenagers from a small town in Ireland, as they navigate love, friendship, and social class. Their bond evolves through high school and into their time at Trinity College, where their roles and dynamics shift dramatically. The novel explores themes of intimacy, identity, and the impact of family on personal relationships. Tone and style: introspective, spare, contemporary. Pacing: slow-burn, character-driven. Themes: class, love, friendship, identity. Setting: contemporary Ireland, primarily Dublin. About the author: Sally Rooney is an Irish author. She is the author of the novels Conversations with Friends (2017), Normal People (2018), Beautiful World, Where Are You (2021), and Intermezzo (2024). The first two works were adapted into the television miniseries Normal People (2020) and Conversations with Friends (2022). Her bestselling novels have sold more than 6 million copies worldwide, have been translated into over 47 languages, and have garnered critical acclaim and commercial success. Literary commentators regard Rooney as one of the foremost millennial writers, and in 2022, Time named her among the 100 most influential people in the world.

title: Mr. Penumbra's 24 Hour Bookstore
author: Robin Sloan
text: Published 2012. Genre: Literary Fiction. Clay Jannon, after losing his tech job during the Great Recession, takes a position at a peculiar 24-hour bookstore in San Francisco. He discovers that the store is a front for a secret society obsessed with an ancient mystery involving books and knowledge. Tone and style: whimsical, tech-savvy, conversational. Pacing: fast-paced, plot-driven. Themes: technology, knowledge, mystery, community. Setting: contemporary San Francisco. About the author: Robin Sloan is an American author. His debut novel, Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore, was published in 2012.

title: We'll Prescribe You a Cat
author: Syou Ishida
text: Published 2024-09-05. Genre: Literary Fiction. The Kokoro Cat Clinic in Kyoto offers emotional support through the companionship of cats to individuals experiencing emotional pain. Each cat assists different patients, helping them navigate their struggles and find healing and self-discovery. The stories of the patients and their feline companions explore themes of hope and personal growth. Tone and style: heartwarming, gentle, reflective. Pacing: measured, character-driven. Themes: healing, companionship, self-discovery, emotional support. Setting: contemporary Kyoto, Japan.

title: The Yiddish Policeman's Union
author: Michael Chabon
text: Published 2006. Genre: Mystery. Set in an alternate history where a Jewish settlement exists in Alaska, this novel follows a homicide detective named Meyer Landsman as he investigates the murder of a fellow resident. The story explores themes of identity, belonging, and the complexities of Jewish culture against a backdrop of noir detective fiction. Tone and style: darkly humorous, richly detailed. Pacing: steady, character-driven. Themes: identity, belonging, cultural heritage. Setting: alternate history Jewish settlement in Alaska. About the author: Michael Chabon is an American novelist, screenwriter, columnist, and short story writer. Born in Washington, D.C., he studied at Carnegie Mellon University for one year before transferring to the University of Pittsburgh, graduating in 1984. He subsequently received a Master of Fine Arts in creative writing from the University of California, Irvine.

title: Rubicon
author: Tom Holland
text: Published 2003. Genre: History. Rubicon explores the transition of Rome from a republic to an empire during the tumultuous period of 49 B.C. It focuses on key historical figures such as Julius Caesar, Cicero, and Cleopatra, illustrating the complexities of Roman society through civil war, political intrigue, and personal rivalries. Tom Holland combines engaging narrative with thorough scholarship to present a vivid portrait of this pivotal era in Roman history. Tone and style: engaging, vivid, scholarly. Pacing: fast-paced, narrative-driven. Themes: political power, civil war, historical transformation. Setting: ancient Rome during the late Republic. About the author: Thomas Stanley Holland is a British actor known for his work in a diverse range of genres. His accolades include a BAFTA Award as well as two Critics' Choice Awards nominations. Holland's films as a leading actor have grossed over $13.1 billion worldwide, making him one of the highest-grossing actors of all time. He was featured on the Forbes 30 Under 30 Europe list of 2019.

title: Smiley's People
author: John Le Carré
text:
